## Overview

The machine learning community currently has no standardized process for documenting datasets. Gebru and colleagues propose "datasheets for datasets," where every dataset be accompanied with a datasheet that documents its motivation, composition, collection process, recommended uses, and so on.

## The Proposal

By analogy to the electronics industry, where every component is accompanied with a datasheet that describes its operating characteristics, test results, recommended uses, and other information, the researchers propose a similar approach for machine learning datasets.

## Purpose and Benefits

Datasheets for datasets will facilitate better communication between dataset creators and dataset consumers, and encourage the machine learning community to prioritize transparency and accountability. 

These datasheets should answer questions that focus on when, where, and how the training data was gathered, its recommended use cases, and, in the case of human-centric datasets, information regarding the subjects' demographics and consent as applicable.

## Publication Details

The paper was submitted on March 23, 2018, with the latest version published on December 1, 2021. The authors developed prototypes of datasheets for two well-known datasets: Labeled Faces in The Wild and the Pang & Lee Polarity Dataset.

Based on the search results, here's what NYC Local Law 144 requires regarding automated employment decision tool bias audits:

## Overview

NYC Local Law 144 of 2021 requires employers and employment agencies that use certain hiring algorithms to commission an annual bias audit. Enforcement began on 5 July 2023, making it one of the earliest US measures to place concrete, testable obligations on AI used in employment.

## Scope

Local Law 144 applies to automated employment decision tools (AEDTs) — broadly, computational tools that substantially assist or replace discretionary decision-making in hiring or promotion. Where an AEDT is used to screen candidates or employees for a position in New York City, the law imposes audit, notice and publication duties.

## Bias Audit Requirements

The key audit requirements include:

- The audit must be independent and impartial, conducted by an auditor that is not involved in using or developing the tool.
- It must be carried out no more than one year before the tool is used.
- It tests the AEDT for disparate impact — assessing how selection or scoring outcomes differ across categories such as sex, and race or ethnicity, and intersections of those categories.
- A bias audit must calculate the "selection rate" for certain race/ethnicity and sex categories and the "impact ratio" comparing the most selected category for each race/ethnicity, sex, and intersectional category.

## Notice and Disclosure Requirements

Covered employers or employment agencies must provide at least 10 days' prior notice that the AEDT will be used and that the candidate or employee may request an alternative selection process or accommodation, as well as at least 10 days' prior notice of the job qualifications and characteristics the AEDT will use to assess the candidate or employee.

## Overview

Colorado's SB 24-205 takes effect February 1, 2026, and covers the use of AI in several contexts including employment, education, lending, healthcare, housing and other services.

## Impact Assessment Requirements

Developers must produce documentation that empowers the person who will deploy the system to complete an impact assessment. Deployers are required to complete an impact assessment of the system.

## Employment-Specific Obligations

While employers may not be developers, they will almost certainly be deployers of high-risk AI systems, particularly in hiring.

Deployers must implement a risk management policy and program, complete an impact assessment of the system, and annually review the deployment of each system to help ensure it is not causing algorithmic discrimination.

SB 24-205 makes clear there is no private right of action under the law, leaving exclusive enforcement to the state attorney general's office.

## High-Risk Classification

Recruitment screening tools, performance monitoring analytics, and absence prediction engines are explicitly listed under EU AI Act Annex III as high-risk AI use cases. Annex III, point 4(a) covers AI systems intended to be used for the recruitment or selection of natural persons, and the regulation covers any system that filters, ranks, scores, or otherwise influences which candidates a human decision-maker sees or considers.

## Compliance Obligations

That classification brings conformity assessments, Fundamental Rights Impact Assessments, technical documentation obligations, human oversight procedures, and a registration requirement in the EU AI Act database.

## Technical Documentation Requirements

Annex IV specifies the exact contents of required technical documentation: general description, intended purpose, version history, interaction with other systems, training data description, validation and testing methodology, accuracy metrics, and known risks. Documentation must cover the system's intended purpose, the training data used (including its sources and demographic characteristics), the performance benchmarks achieved, the bias testing methodology and results, and the human oversight mechanism in place.

## Training Data Requirements

Training, validation, and testing datasets must be relevant, representative, and free from errors that could produce discriminatory outputs.

## Compliance Timeline

The full high-risk obligations under Chapter III were originally set to apply from August 2, 2026, but the EU's Digital Omnibus initiative delayed the Annex III compliance deadline to December 2, 2027.

## Overview

Article 53(1)(d) of the EU AI Act requires providers of general-purpose AI (GPAI) models to publish a sufficiently detailed public summary about the content used for training based on a template provided by the AI Office.

The stated goal of this obligation is to increase transparency regarding the data used for training GPAI models, and to enable relevant stakeholders to exercise their rights, especially regarding IP, copyright, and data protection. On 24 July 2025, the European Commission's AI Office released the long-awaited template for the public summary of training content used in general-purpose AI (GPAI) models. ## Scope

All providers of GPAI models, including the providers of free and open-source licenses, are required to fulfill this obligation.

Each summary discloses, per modality (Text / Image / Audio / Video), a banded training-data size, the data-acquisition cut-off, and yes/no flags per data-source category.

Here are the search results on EEOC guidance regarding disparate impact, Title VII, algorithmic hiring, and the four-fifths rule:

## Key Concepts

Disparate or adverse impact refers to an employer's use of a facially neutral employment selection procedure or test that has a disproportionately large negative impact on individuals based on characteristics protected under Title VII, such as race, color, religion, sex, or national origin.

## Algorithmic Tools and Title VII

The EEOC treats employer use of algorithmic decision-making tools as an employment "selection procedure" under Title VII, subject to the EEOC's Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures adopted in 1979. Employers must ensure that their selection procedures when using algorithmic decision-making tools do not result in a disparate or adverse impact under Title VII—unless they can establish that the use of these tools is "job-related and consistent with business necessity," and there is no less-discriminatory alternative that is equally effective.

## The Four-Fifths Rule

The "four-fifths rule" states that "one rate is substantially different than another if their ratio is less than four-fifths" (or 80 percent). Under the four-fifths rule, adverse impact is generally indicated where a "selection rate" for any protected characteristic is less than 80% (four-fifths) of the rate of the group with the highest selection rate.

## Important Limitations

The EEOC cautioned employers that the four-fifths rule is not always an appropriate test and that smaller differences in selection rates may indicate adverse impact. The four-fifths rule is "merely a rule of thumb" and reliance on the rule is not dispositive. The use of the four-fifths rule may be "inappropriate" in certain circumstances because, for example, the data may not be sufficient to provide a statistically significant assessment.

# NYC Local Law 144: Compliance and Effectiveness Findings

## Compliance Rates

The research revealed dramatically low compliance with the law's disclosure requirements:

- Out of 267 employers with open NYC jobs, researchers found only **14 audit reports (5%)** and **12 notices (4%)** about automated decision-making tools
- This suggests the vast majority of affected employers are either not using algorithmic hiring tools or failing to disclose their use

## What Gets Published

When audits were posted, they predominantly showed favorable results. Researchers noted that "most showed the tools didn't run afoul of the threshold for bias that the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission uses as a rule of thumb." The authors theorize this reflects selective disclosure—employers likely publish favorable audits while withholding evidence of bias to avoid litigation.

## Achievement of Anti-Discrimination Goals

The law falls far short of its objectives. Student investigators found the audit-search experience was "challenging, time-consuming, and frustrating," with audits scattered across various website locations. If trained searchers struggled to locate disclosures, average job-seekers presumably would too.

The research concludes the law "hasn't lived up to its goals" because excessive employer discretion in interpretation undermines transparency and enforcement.

# NYC Local Law 144 Compliance: Key Findings

## Compliance Rates

The study found strikingly low compliance with the law's transparency requirements:

- **Audit reports**: Only 5% of employers with NYC job listings (14 of 267) published bias audits
- **Transparency notices**: Just 4% (12 of 267) posted required notices to job seekers
- **Complete compliance**: Only 11 employers published both documents

## Why Accountability Failed

The researchers identified a critical structural flaw they termed **"null compliance"**—a situation where "the absence of evidence of compliance cannot be ascertained as non-compliance because the investigator lacks the information to determine if the regulated party's actions or products are in scope of the regulation."

### Primary Causes:

**1. Excessive employer discretion**: The law granted employers wide latitude to self-determine whether their systems fell under its scope, making it impossible to verify actual AEDT deployment rates.

**2. Poor information accessibility**: Trained student investigators struggled to locate disclosures within 30-minute searches, averaging 17-19 website pages. The researchers concluded that "job seekers will only rarely encounter audit reports or transparency notices even when available."

**3. Confusing presentation**: Required information was buried among other legal disclaimers and diversity statements, creating ambiguity about applicability.

**4. Publication bias**: 96% of published audit reports showed impact ratios above the 0.8 threshold, suggesting employers withheld unfavorable results to avoid litigation exposure—a rational response given the law lacks enforcement mechanisms or legal safe harbors.

The paper concludes the transparency mandate ultimately failed to enable informed job-seeker choice or meaningful regulatory oversight.

1	<!-- GENERATED — DO NOT EDIT. Source: shared/spine/references/output-template.md. Regenerate via: scripts/sync-content.py --write. -->
2	
3	# First Principles Analysis Output Template
4	
5	> **Note:** This is the full annotated template with complete section guidance, type
6	> definitions, and prescriptions. A condensed skeleton showing just the required section
7	> names and chain format lives resident in the agent body (`SKILL.md` on the skill surface, `agents/first-principles.md` on the agent surface) for quick reference. Come here
8	> for the complete instructions when authoring or reviewing an analysis.
9	
10	## How to Use This Template
11	
12	This template is a **strict-shape document**. All six sections must be present in the fixed order below. No section may be omitted.
13	
14	If a section has no genuine content for a given analysis — because the problem is simple, the domain has no relevant dead ends, or the section truly does not apply — mark it with the honest-depth escape valve:
15	
16	> `Nothing material here — [reason explaining why this section has no content for this particular analysis and that the omission is justified, not lazy]`
17	
18	The section heading must still appear. The escape valve exists to prevent box-ticking fabrication: it is always better to write `Nothing material here — [reason]` than to fill a section with words that say nothing.
19	
20	**Section order (fixed):**
21	1. Problem Essence
22	2. Assumptions Table
23	3. Ground Truths
24	4. Derivation Chains
25	5. Abandoned Reasoning
26	6. Conclusion
27	
28	### Document order
29	
30	The delivered file is not just these six sections — it is assembled in one absolute order: a
31	short `## Answer` block; then sections 1 through 6 above, in the fixed order and unchanged; then
32	one `## Appendix — process output` heading; then every process-output block produced during the
33	run, in the order produced, each keeping its own existing top-level heading.
34	
35	The `## Answer` block sits above section 1 and carries three bold lead-ins: `**Recommendation:**`
36	(1–3 sentences restating §6's `**Recommended approach:**`), `**Band (from §6):**` (§6's own
37	`**Confidence:**` band, copied verbatim), and `**Would change it:**` (the evidence or verification
38	§6 names as capable of moving the band or the recommendation). Each lead-in cites at least one
39	chain inline — `(chain Cn)` — and every chain it cites is one §6 already cites for the claim being
40	restated: the Answer states nothing §6 does not already state with the same chain. It is at most
41	120 words, is written last from the final §6 text, and is not a seventh output section. Before the
42	file is assembled, each Answer line is confirmed to restate a §6 claim and name its chain; a line
43	that does not is cut, not softened.
44	
45	**Nothing about the environment enters the document.** The six sections above are the whole deliverable, and none of them has a slot for the state of the session that produced it. Tooling, connector, authorisation, permission, quota, configuration, model, harness and transcript state are all environment state, and none of it belongs in the analysis — not in a section, not appended after §6, not as a footnote. This exclusion is about environment-state *content*, never about physical position in the file: the trailing `## Appendix — process output` sits after §6 and carries process output — the Self-Audit Gate's verdict blocks, the closure ledger, the self-audit scan, the adversarial pass record — none of which is environment state, and its presence there does not reopen this rule. The class is *any* fact about the machinery rather than about the problem; it is not a list of forbidden words, and a new kind of environment fact is covered by this rule on the day it first exists. A prefix such as "Unrelated to this analysis", "Separately" or "Note:" does not make such a paragraph admissible — it marks the writer as already knowing the paragraph does not belong, which is the point at which it is dropped rather than labelled. Where environment state genuinely blocked the analysis, it is already disclosed in its proper place: a failed reference read under the template's own disclosure rule, and an unmet evidence need as a `?`-marked input carried into the Assumptions Table and named on the affected `**Confidence:**` line. Environment state that blocked nothing is reported to the user outside the deliverable, after the document ends, or not at all.
46	
47	---
48	
49	## 1. Problem Essence
50	
51	State the core problem in a single sentence — not the symptoms, not the solution space, but the irreducible question the analysis must answer.
52	
53	**Core problem:** [One sentence. Strip away implementation details and surface the underlying question.]
54	
55	**Success criteria:** [Measurable, observable outcomes that would confirm the problem is solved. A skeptic must be able to verify these without asking for further clarification.]
56	
57	---
58	
59	## 2. Assumptions Table
60	
61	List every assumption — explicit and implicit — that the analysis rests on. Classify each by type and apply the prescribed treatment. An assumption omitted from this table is an assumption that will propagate unchallenged through every later step.
62	
63	| Assumption | Type | Treatment | Verdict | Verification |
64	|------------|------|-----------|---------|--------------|
65	| [Assumption text] | [physical law / current constraint / convention / untested belief] | [prescribed action per type — see below] | [Accept / Challenge / Discard] — [justification/reason] | [source, or "unverified — flagged" if used in a chain per D-07] |
66	
67	**These five columns are the whole table — no ID column.** Assumptions are referred to by the
68	`[Assumes: A-N]` marks the chains carry and by the `A-N` labels used in the Assumption Audit
69	scan; adding a sixth ID column to this table duplicates that identity in a second place, and two
70	places that name the same thing drift. A run that adds one is deviating from this template even
71	though nothing rejects it today.
72	
73	### Type Definitions and Prescribed Treatments
74	
75	**physical law** — a constraint imposed by physics, mathematics, or formal logic that cannot change regardless of context or decisions made.
76	Prescribed treatment: accept as a ground-truth candidate and record it in the Ground Truths section.
77	
78	**current constraint** — a real limitation that applies now but could change (budget, team size, regulatory environment, technology availability).
79	Prescribed treatment: record the expiry conditions — what would have to change for this constraint to no longer hold. Do not treat it as permanent.
80	
81	**convention** — a practice or standard that exists because it has been adopted, not because it is physically or logically required.
82	Prescribed treatment: explicitly challenge the convention before accepting it. "We do it this way" is not a justification.
83	
84	**untested belief** — a claim held as true that has not been empirically verified in the context of this analysis.
85	Prescribed treatment: verify it, or flag it unverified. An untested belief used in a derivation chain must be marked with the `GT-N?` notation (see Ground Truths) and any conclusion depending on it inherits a confidence caveat.
86	
87	### Stakes-Escalation Rule
88	
89	The higher the stakes of the conclusion resting on an assumption, the more that assumption must be pushed toward physical law or verified ground truth status. Classification drives the method — it does not merely label.
90	
91	### Verdict Vocabulary
92	
93	The Verdict cell is a token prefix followed by an em-dash and the justification — the bare
94	token leads so it stays matchable, and the em-dash prose carries the reasoning. **The separator
95	is an em-dash, never a colon.** `Accept: the figure is audited` puts the token and the reasoning
96	on one side of a punctuation mark that appears throughout ordinary prose, so the cell stops being
97	matchable — which is the whole property the token-first form exists to provide. Measured: a single
98	run using the colon form scored ten non-conforming verdict cells at once. The em-dash is not a
99	stylistic preference here; it is the delimiter:
100	
101	- **Accept** — the assumption survives challenge and may be used in the analysis (e.g., "Accept — survives P2 challenge; physical-law backed by GT-1")
102	- **Challenge** — the assumption is questionable; probe further before use (e.g., "Challenge — vendor benchmark unverified, flagged GT-5?")
103	- **Discard** — the assumption is false or irrelevant; remove from the reasoning chain (e.g., "Discard — contradicted by GT-2, no longer load-bearing")
104	
105	**A current-constraint verdict records its expiry at the point of use.** An assumption classified `current constraint` is accepted only until that constraint lapses; the verdict cell says when. The expiry belongs in the em-dash justification and never in the token slot — the token slot carries one of the three tokens above and nothing else.
106	
107	**Conforming — a current constraint recording its expiry:**
108	
109	```text
110	Accept — expires at term end (1 or 3 years); until then the constraint is contractual, not physical
111	```
112	
113	**Non-conforming — the expiry hoisted into the token slot:**
114	
115	```text
116	Current constraint (expires at term end) — contractual, not physical
117	```
118	
119	The vocabulary above is unchanged because run 3 rendered four current-constraint rows conformingly on the identical prompt by putting the expiry in the justification — this is a worked example, not a schema change.
120	
121	---
122	
123	## 3. Ground Truths
124	
125	List the irreducible, verified facts the analysis builds on. Each ground truth carries a stable identifier used by the Derivation Chains section. Once assigned, an ID does not change.
126	
127	A ground truth must pass this test: it is a fact that is true regardless of what solution is chosen, verifiable independently of the analysis, and not derived from another item on this list.
128	
129	Every ground truth carries a **provenance label** answering one question: *did this analysis read the asserted figure or wording in the cited source?* The answer decides the suffix. A citation being present is not verification — a citation can name a real document and be wrong about what is in it.
130	
131	**Verified ground truth form** (provenance `read-at-source` — no suffix):
132	
133	- **GT-1** [fact text] — source: [verification source — data, measurement, published spec, direct observation]; read-at-source: [page, table, section, or quoted passage where the figure was read]
134	- **GT-2** [fact text] — source: [verification source]; read-at-source: [where read]
135	
136	**Delegate-reported ground truth form** (provenance `reported-by-delegate` — `?` required):
137	
138	- **GT-3?** [fact text] — cited to: [source the delegate named]; reported-by-delegate: [which sub-agent, search, or summary supplied it] — cited source not opened by this analysis
139	
140	**Unverified ground truth form (D-07)** (provenance `unverified` — `?` required):
141	
142	- **GT-4?** [fact text] — unverified: [specific reason the fact could not be verified in this analysis]
143	
144	The `?` suffix signals that this ground truth has not been read at its source — whether because it is an untested belief or because a delegate reported it and nobody opened the citation. Any conclusion depending on a `GT-N?` input inherits a confidence caveat in the Derivation Chains section. The analysis may proceed with such inputs — but the uncertainty must be visible.
145	
146	**The `?` is the default.** Drop it only when the read-at-source location can be named. A delegate report counts as read-at-source only when it quotes the source's own wording and that quote was checked — not when it merely supplies a well-formed citation.
147	
148	**Provenance summary (required):** enumerate the `?`-marked ground truths **by ID**, and for every unsuffixed ground truth feeding a HIGH-confidence chain, name its read-at-source location. Write the list, not a number:
149	
150	```text
151	?-marked: GT-2, GT-5, GT-9, GT-14 (4 of 22)
152	Read-at-source: GT-3 — 45 CFR 164.514(b)(2)(i), subsections (A)/(B)/(R) quoted verbatim
153	```
154	
155	A stated integer does not satisfy this — an integer cannot be checked against the list it summarizes, and an enumeration can. Where a count and its enumeration disagree, **the enumeration governs.** Neither an empty enumeration nor a count of zero satisfies this on its own; the named locations are the auditable part.
156	
157	IDs are stable once assigned. GT-3 remains GT-3 throughout the document even if GT-3 is later verified or discarded.
158	
159	---
160	
161	## 4. Derivation Chains
162	
163	Show how the ground truths combine into conclusions. Every conclusion offered in this analysis must have exactly one chain here — no more (no redundant restatement), no fewer (no orphaned conclusions).
164	
165	**Chain numbering convention.** Number each `### Conclusion:` block in this section `C1`,
166	`C2`, ... in document order (e.g., `### Conclusion C1: [Conclusion text]`). The §6→§4
167	closure ledger (the agent body — `SKILL.md` on the skill surface, `agents/first-principles.md` on the agent surface — "Before presenting conclusions") cites these IDs when mapping a
168	Conclusion-section (section 6) claim back to the chain in this section that established it.
169	
170	**Chain format:**
171	
172	```text
173	GT-N + GT-M → [intermediate claim] → [conclusion]
174	```
175	
176	The one-line form is the degenerate case, used only when the whole chain fits on one physical line; a chain that does not fit uses the head-plus-arrow-led form, and a hop is split rather than continued on a second line.
177	
178	Each chain must contain at least one intermediate step. A chain that goes directly from its head inputs to conclusion is incomplete — the intermediate is where the reasoning happens. The intermediate must be a new claim that could not be stated from any single head input alone. If no intermediate can be stated, the conclusion is either a restatement of a head input (trivial) or a reasoning step is missing.
179	
180	**No-wrap rule.** A hop occupies exactly one physical line. Every line after the head begins with `→` and carries exactly one complete hop; a hop is never broken across physical lines. A chain needing more hops continues on further arrow-led lines. A hop too long for comfort is SPLIT, not wrapped — the analysis renders as Markdown, so a long hop soft-wraps for the reader without breaking the form.
181	
182	```text
183	GT-1 ([brief fact label]) + GT-6 ([brief fact label])
184	→ [intermediate claim]
185	→ [further intermediate]
186	→ [conclusion]
187	```
188	
189	**Head-input rule.** The head line lists the inputs the chain consumes: each is a `GT-N` identifier (`GT-N?` when the ground truth is unverified) or a `Cn` identifier, optionally followed by a parenthesized gloss, joined to the next by `+`. The first `→` closes the head. An input carrying unparenthesized prose — `C2's threshold` — is not an identifier and does not parse; write `C2 (threshold)` in every position. The mechanical form check detects that violation only when the prose input is the last one before the first `→`; in an earlier position the check matches the well-formed remainder and scores the head conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach.
190	
191	```text
192	GT-1? ([brief fact label]) + C2 ([brief fact label])
193	→ [intermediate claim]
194	→ [conclusion]
195	```
196	
197	The head grammar governs the head line only. A hop is prose: `C2's saving` is fine after the first `→`, and is not an input reference. One exception: a hop must not begin with a `GT-N` identifier, which the form check reads as the head of a new chain and which therefore ends this one — write `→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term`, not `→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term`. The form check detects that violation only while fewer than two hops precede it; in a later position the check matches the preceding hops and scores the chain conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach.
198	
199	The mechanical form check additionally rejects a chain whose head or first hop closes its own sentence before the next `→`: it reads the following arrow-led line as a new statement and ends the chain there, so a chain satisfying every rule above is scored malformed for that reason alone. The check reaches only that position — a hop that closes its own sentence from the second hop onward does not change the verdict — which is why intermediate hops carry no terminal punctuation in this project's worked examples.
200	
201	**Conforming — head, then one hop per line:**
202	
203	```text
204	GT-1 (Lambda $/GB-s, AWS pricing) + GT-6 (Fargate $/vCPU-hr, AWS pricing)
205	→ Lambda costs 2.10× per unit of actual compute
206	→ sustained workloads belong on Fargate
207	```
208	
209	**Non-conforming — a hop broken across physical lines:**
210	
211	```text
212	GT-1 (Lambda $/GB-s, AWS pricing) + GT-6 (Fargate $/vCPU-hr, AWS pricing)
213	→ Lambda costs 2.10× per unit of actual compute
214	  once idle-time billing is included
215	→ sustained workloads belong on Fargate
216	```
217	
218	The continuation line does not begin with `→`, so the chain terminates at the head's first hop and what remains reads as an incomplete chain.
219	
220	**Non-conforming — the same hops rendered as a numbered list:**
221	
222	```text
223	1. GT-1 (Lambda $/GB-s, AWS pricing) + GT-6 (Fargate $/vCPU-hr, AWS pricing)
224	2. Lambda costs 2.10× per unit of actual compute
225	3. sustained workloads belong on Fargate
226	```
227	
228	A numbered list restates each hop as its own GT-headed one-hop chain, which reads as several incomplete chains rather than one complete one — the intermediate steps stop being connected to the conclusion they build toward.
229	
230	**Non-conforming — an input carrying unparenthesized prose:**
231	
232	```text
233	GT-13? (bill composition unknown) + GT-12? (duty cycle unknown) + C2's threshold
234	→ target quantity: fraction of total AWS bill removed by the migration
235	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
236	```
237	
238	`C2's threshold` is not an identifier — it is a possessive prose phrase — so the head does not parse; the third input must be written `C2 (threshold)`.
239	
240	**Conforming — the same head with the upstream chain as an input:**
241	
242	```text
243	GT-13? (bill composition unknown) + GT-12? (duty cycle unknown) + C2 (threshold)
244	→ target quantity: fraction of total AWS bill removed by the migration
245	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
246	```
247	
248	Exactly one token differs from the block above: a `Cn` identifier with a parenthesized gloss is an admissible head input, on equal footing with a `GT-N` identifier.
249	
250	**Conforming — a chain consuming only upstream conclusions:**
251	
252	```text
253	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold) + C4 (unconditional, zero code change) + C5 (~73% ceiling, no execution-model change)
254	→ C4 and C5 deliver verified savings that do not depend on any property of your workload
255	→ C2's saving depends entirely on a duty-cycle figure nobody has measured
256	```
257	
258	A head may consist entirely of `Cn` inputs with no `GT-N` term. The second hop's `C2's saving` is prose, not a head input — the head-only scope note is what permits it here.
259	
260	**Non-conforming, and undetected by the form check — the same prose input in a non-final position:**
261	
262	```text
263	GT-13? (bill composition unknown) + C2's threshold + GT-12? (duty cycle unknown)
264	→ target quantity: fraction of total AWS bill removed by the migration
265	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
266	```
267	
268	This head breaks the same rule as the non-conforming block above and is equally non-conforming, but the mechanical form check scores it conforming — with a well-formed input still to its right the check matches from `GT-12?` onward and never reaches `C2's threshold`. Write `C2 (threshold)` wherever the input sits; the rule is the contract, and the check is a partial instrument for it.
269	
270	**Non-conforming — a hop beginning with a GT-N identifier:**
271	
272	```text
273	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
274	→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term in both estimates
275	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
276	```
277	
278	The second line reads as the head of a new chain because it begins with a `GT-N` identifier, so this chain ends after its head and what remains is an incomplete chain — the possessive is not the problem, the leading identifier is.
279	
280	**Conforming — the same hop with the identifier moved off the front:**
281	
282	```text
283	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
284	→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term in both estimates
285	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
286	```
287	
288	Exactly one clause is reordered and the chain is whole again; naming a ground truth inside a hop is fine, leading with its identifier is not.
289	
290	**Non-conforming, and undetected by the form check — the GT-led hop in a later position:**
291	
292	```text
293	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
294	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
295	→ the second reading is the binding one
296	→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term in both estimates
297	```
298	
299	This hop breaks the same rule as the non-conforming block above and is equally non-conforming, but the mechanical form check scores it conforming — the check has already satisfied its two-arrow requirement on the hops that precede it, so the leading identifier ends the chain there without changing the verdict. Write `→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term in both estimates` wherever the hop sits; the rule is the contract, and the check is a partial instrument for it.
300	
301	**Non-conforming — the first hop closing its own sentence:**
302	
303	```text
304	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
305	→ C1's saving is unconditional and does not depend on workload shape.
306	→ C2's saving is real only above the duty-cycle threshold this estimate assumes
307	```
308	
309	This chain violates none of R1-R9 — every input parses, every hop states one inference, no hop leads with a `GT-N` identifier — and is scored malformed anyway, because the mechanical form check ends the chain the moment the first hop closes its own sentence, before its two-arrow requirement is satisfied, and never reaches the well-formed hop that follows.
310	
311	**Conforming — the same chain with the first hop's terminal period removed:**
312	
313	```text
314	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
315	→ C1's saving is unconditional and does not depend on workload shape
316	→ C2's saving is real only above the duty-cycle threshold this estimate assumes
317	```
318	
319	Exactly one character differs from the block above: the terminal period. Removing it, and nothing else, restores the two-arrow match the check requires.
320	
321	**Non-conforming, and undetected by the form check — the same period moved to a later hop:**
322	
323	```text
324	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
325	→ C1's saving is unconditional and does not depend on workload shape
326	→ the migration case does not rest on C1 alone
327	→ C2's saving is real only above the duty-cycle threshold this estimate assumes.
328	```
329	
330	This block breaks the identical rule one hop later and is equally non-conforming, but the mechanical form check scores it conforming — with two hops already matched before the closing sentence is reached, the check has satisfied its two-arrow requirement and the sentence-closing period on the third hop has no following line left to block. Write the closing hop with no terminal punctuation wherever it sits; the rule is the contract, and the check is a partial instrument for it.
331	
332	**One-inference rule.** A hop states exactly ONE inference. If a hop joins two claims with "and", or carries a parenthetical that could stand as its own claim, it is two hops — split it.
333	
334	TELL (not the rule): a hop past ~200 characters is almost always two hops. Measure the hop, then split — do not wrap it, and do not trim words to hit a number.
335	
336	Inline annotations (`*[Assumes: A14 — …]*`) attach to the end of the hop line they qualify and do not start a new hop.
337	
338	### Converting structured-technique outputs into chains
339	
340	Structured-technique outputs (trade-off matrices, second-order effect lists) do not appear in this section as-is — each converts into the chain format above using the rule for its technique below. This subsection is the single source of truth for the conversion; the per-technique Handoff sections point back here rather than restating it, so future structured techniques extend this one place.
341	
342	**Trade-off matrix → one chain.** A trade-off matrix collapses into ONE chain whose intermediate cites the winning weighted total and whose endpoint names a single recommended option:
343	
344	```text
345	GT-refs (criteria's factual basis) → weighted totals (the winning total vs. the runner-up, naming the high-weight criteria that drive it) → recommended option
346	```
347	
348	Example: `GT-2 + GT-5 (criteria facts) → weighted totals: B=82 > A=64, driven by reliability×warranty → recommend B`. The full matrix stays in the technique's own output — this subsection carries only the single collapsed chain, never the matrix re-expressed row-by-row (that would violate the one-chain-per-conclusion rule above). An exact tie between weighted totals still resolves to a single named recommended option; a tie must not produce a multi-option chain endpoint. **Exact-tie tiebreak (deterministic):** on an exact tie, prefer the option with fewer `GT-N?` (unverified) inputs among its winning criteria; if still tied, name both totals in the chain intermediate but select the first-listed option as the chain endpoint, and flag the tie explicitly in the Conclusion section's confidence line.
349	
350	**Second-order effect list → order-marked extension.** A second-order effect list extends the parent chain IN PLACE as additional order-marked steps, each carrying the same evidentiary discipline as the first-order steps that produced the conclusion:
351	
352	```text
353	GT-N → first-order conclusion →[2nd] [2nd-order effect] →[3rd] [3rd-order effect] (contradicts GT-M → back to Phase 2)
354	```
355	
356	Example: `GT-1 → first-order conclusion →[2nd] flag-config surface grows →[3rd] flag debt accumulates (contradicts GT-4 → back to P2)`. The order marks (`[2nd]`, `[3rd]`) make the extension's sequence legible. A contradicting effect routes the conclusion back to Phase 2 — never directly to Phase 3 or past Phase 2. A pass that surfaces no non-contradicting downstream effect leaves the parent chain unextended — a clean no-op, not an error.
357	
358	### Confidence levels, defined
359	
360	`HIGH`, `MEDIUM` and `LOW` name how much of a chain is **outstanding** — not how strongly the analysis believes its conclusion. Three axes decide the band, each answerable by inspecting what the chain already carries on the page:
361	
362	- **Inputs** — the provenance of every identifier on the head line: an unsuffixed `GT-N` with a named read-at-source location, a `?`-marked ground truth, or a `Cn` carrying its own band.
363	- **Inference** — whether each hop the chain's endpoint depends on follows from the line above it, or needs a premise supplied by an `[Assumes: A-N]` annotation.
364	- **Rivals** — whether a competing conclusion from the same ground truths survives, and what rules it out. Section 5 is where the ruling-out is written down, so a chain answers this axis by pointing at its own Abandoned Reasoning entry as readily as by carrying the rival on its confidence line.
365	
366	**The band is the lowest the three axes license.** A chain is not HIGH because two of them are clean.
367	
368	**HIGH — nothing on this chain is outstanding.** Every identifier on the head line is an unsuffixed `GT-N` whose read-at-source location is named, or a `Cn` itself rated HIGH; every hop the endpoint depends on follows from the line above it by deduction, by arithmetic that recomputes when redone independently of the chain text, or by a regularity cited to an unsuffixed ground truth; and the strongest rival conclusion the analysis considered is named — on this confidence line or in a section 5 entry this chain points to — together with the ground truth or chain that rules it out, that ruling-out input itself unsuffixed. A chain whose endpoint a live alternative still contests is unexamined, not certain: it is MEDIUM at best.
369	
370	An `[Assumes: A-N]` annotation on a hop shorts the Inference axis **unless** the confidence line says what becomes of the endpoint when that assumption fails and the endpoint still stands — *"A2 is that the CDN'd assets are versioned; if they were not, the CDN result would be weaker evidence still, so the conclusion is unaffected"*. An annotation on a hop that only qualifies a second-order extension, and not the endpoint, is outside this axis and the chain says which case it is. Stating the sensitivity is the work; an unexamined assumption is not the same thing as one whose falsity has been priced.
371	
372	The Rivals axis is answered when a section 5 entry names a competing conclusion to this chain's endpoint and the chain or ground truth that ruled it out, or when the endpoint is itself a ruling-out — a chain establishing that some option does not work has already done the rival's work and does not need a rival of its own. It is short when a competing conclusion has been raised anywhere in the analysis and nothing settles it, and when the analysis reaches a positive recommendation with no section 5 content bearing on it at all.
373	
374	**MEDIUM — exactly one axis is short, and the shortfall is named and bounded.** One of: an identifier on the head line is `?`-marked or is a `Cn` rated MEDIUM; or at most one hop the endpoint depends on rests on a stated `[Assumes: A-N]` premise whose failure the chain has not priced; or a rival to the endpoint is live and nothing in the analysis settles it. The confidence line names which axis is short, names the specific input, hop or rival, and states what would close it — the verification that would remove an input as a cause of the downgrade, the evidence that would establish an assumed premise, or the observation that would settle between this conclusion and its rival. A MEDIUM chain is one whose weakness a reader can point at.
375	
376	**LOW — the shortfall is unbounded, or more than one axis is short.** Two or more axes short at once; or an input is `?` with no verification path available; or a hop's missing premise cannot be stated as an assumption at all, so the analysis cannot say what would make the step valid; or a rival survives that no available observation would settle. A LOW chain is reportable, and a conclusion resting on it alone is not actionable.
377	
378	**Calibration rule.** Each rating is the highest its inputs, hops and rivals license, **and no higher**. Rating above what the axes license over-claims. Rating below it is a defect of the same kind: a chain meeting HIGH on all three axes and written MEDIUM misreports the analysis's own strength, and a document whose every chain carries the same defensive band tells a reader nothing about which parts to trust. Criterion 5 scores calibration, not altitude — an analysis whose every band is the one its axes license is Rigorous whether its conclusion is HIGH, MEDIUM or LOW.
379	
380	**The caps are consequences, not extra rules.** The unverified-input rule (D-07) below and the ceiling at the lowest-rated chain a head cites are what the Inputs axis says, restated for the two cases that occur most often; they are the fast check, and these definitions are what they check for. A cap never licenses a band on its own — it bounds from above, and the band is still the lowest any of the three axes licenses.
381	
382	**Confidence pre-check (Inputs axis).** Directly above every `**Confidence:**` line — each §4 chain's and the §6 Conclusion's — write one `**Pre-check:**` line, with nothing between it and the `**Confidence:**` line it checks:
383	
384	```text
385	**Pre-check:** head GT-1, GT-3?, C2 (MEDIUM) · ?-marked: GT-3? · lowest cited: MEDIUM · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
386	**Confidence:** MEDIUM — GT-3? is unverified; …
387	```
388	
389	Four fields, separated by ` · `: `head` lists every identifier on the chain's head line (the part before the first `→`), in order, comma-separated, a `?` suffix kept (`GT-3?`), each `Cn` followed by its own stated band in parentheses (`C2 (MEDIUM)`) — for the §6 roll-up, `head` is every chain the Conclusion rests on, each with its band, plus any `GT-N?` the Conclusion rests on directly. `?-marked` lists the `?`-suffixed identifiers from `head`, comma-separated, or the token `none`. `lowest cited` is the lowest band among the `Cn` in `head`, or `none` when `head` cites no chain. `Inputs ceiling` is the Inputs axis's bound: `LOW` if `lowest cited` is LOW; otherwise `MEDIUM` if `?-marked` is not `none` or `lowest cited` is MEDIUM; otherwise `HIGH`.
390	
391	This is the Inputs axis of "Confidence levels, defined" made procedural — Inference and Rivals are not scored on this line, and can only lower the band further. The ceiling bounds from above, as the caps-are-consequences paragraph above states; the `**Confidence:**` label may equal it or sit below it, and never above it — a below-ceiling label is explained by the Confidence line itself, not by the pre-check. In §6, the pre-check line is itself a Conclusion-section claim under the Claim inventory rule below, and it is cited by the chains its own `head` names.
392	
393	### Conclusion C1: [Conclusion text]
394	
395	GT-N ([brief fact label, source]) + GT-M ([brief fact label, source])
396	→ [intermediate claim — a new inference statable from combining GT-N and GT-M but from neither alone]
397	→ [conclusion — the claim this chain establishes]
398	
399	**Pre-check:** head [every head identifier; each Cn with its band, e.g. C2 (MEDIUM)] · ?-marked: [the GT-N? identifiers, or none] · lowest cited: [lowest Cn band, or none] · Inputs ceiling: [HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW]
400	**Confidence:** [HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW]
401	[If MEDIUM or LOW: name each GT-N? input with the verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade; name each Cn on this chain's head rated below HIGH, which need not be re-explained here; and give each downgrade cause belonging to this chain itself — for example a weak inference step or an absent-fails derivation — with what would remove it as a cause of the downgrade or a stated reason no verification path exists (the validation-rubric absent-fails EXCEPT clause, for an absent-fails derivation, or an explicit account of why no available evidence settles that cause).]
402	
403	**Unverified input rule (D-07):** A chain that includes any `GT-N?` input must end with a MEDIUM or LOW confidence line. The line must name the unverified input and state the verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade. A HIGH confidence claim cannot rest on an unverified ground truth. A chain is also rated no higher than the lowest-rated chain its head cites — the stated confidence label of each `Cn` on its head line, the part before the first `→`. This is a ceiling: it bounds the rating from above and is never a reason to rate a chain HIGH, and a cited chain rated MEDIUM under a validation-rubric EXCEPT clause still caps every chain that cites it. Every MEDIUM or LOW confidence line explains only its own chain's rating, so its validity never depends on how far away a cap originates. The line names each `GT-N?` input with the verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade. It names each `Cn` on the chain's head rated below HIGH and need not re-explain that `Cn`, whose own confidence line carries the explanation, so no line has to trace a cited chain's lineage. For each downgrade cause belonging to the chain itself — for example a weak inference step or an absent-fails derivation — the line states what would remove it as a cause of the downgrade or a stated reason no verification path exists. A stated reason is the validation-rubric absent-fails EXCEPT clause, for an absent-fails derivation, or an explicit account of why no available evidence settles that cause; "speculative" is never such a reason. The validation-rubric absent-fails EXCEPT clause is the only clause that can stand in for a verification path, and naming any other clause, including the speculative EXCEPT clause, stands in for nothing. A chain cited on another chain's head is load-bearing, so the rubric's speculative EXCEPT clause no longer covers it, and the cited chain's own confidence line states its verification path; a speculative chain with no verification path is not cited on another chain's head, and stays speculative or moves to Abandoned Reasoning (§5).
404	
405	---
406	
407	## 5. Abandoned Reasoning
408	
409	Record every reasoning path that was explored and discarded. This section is required in every analysis. Dead ends are not failures — they are part of the reasoning record and save future analysts from re-exploring paths that have already been ruled out.
410	
411	### Dead End: [Name of discarded path]
412	
413	**What was tried:** [Brief description of the reasoning path that was pursued.]
414	
415	**Why abandoned:** [The specific failure — assumption false, contradicts a ground truth, assumption classification too weak to anchor the chain, conclusion circular, intermediate could not be established, speculative with no verification path (so not cited on another chain's head), etc. Be precise: "we ran out of time" is not a valid abandonment reason.]
416	
417	**What it ruled out:** [What this dead end saves the reader from re-exploring. A well-documented dead end is as valuable as a live conclusion.]
418	
419	If no reasoning was abandoned, write:
420	
421	`Nothing material here — all reasoning paths pursued led to the conclusion above. [Optional: describe the problem's constraint space that made alternative paths infeasible.]`
422	
423	The escape valve still satisfies D-03. Do not omit the heading.
424	
425	---
426	
427	## 6. Conclusion
428	
429	Summarize the analysis result. The Conclusion section synthesizes what the Derivation Chains established — it does not introduce new claims or reasoning.
430	
431	**Recommended approach:** [Description of the recommended course of action, decision, or design choice.]
432	
433	**Key insight:** [The non-obvious finding the first-principles analysis revealed — what reasoning by analogy or convention would have missed.]
434	
435	**Trade-offs acknowledged:** [What is being accepted, deprioritized, or deferred as a result of this recommendation. No recommendation is free of trade-offs.]
436	
437	**Pre-check:** head [each chain the Conclusion rests on with its band, e.g. C1 (MEDIUM), C3 (HIGH); plus any GT-N? it rests on directly] · ?-marked: [ids, or none] · lowest cited: [lowest band, or none] · Inputs ceiling: [HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW]
438	**Confidence:** [HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW]
439	
440	If Confidence is MEDIUM or LOW: name each chain contributing to the Conclusion that is rated below HIGH, and each `GT-N?` input the Conclusion rests on directly with the verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade. The line need not restate a named chain's verification path or no-path reason; the named chain's own §4 confidence line carries it. Give any downgrade cause belonging to the Conclusion itself with what would remove it as a cause of the downgrade or a stated reason no verification path exists, as §4 defines. A MEDIUM or LOW conclusion without this explanation does not satisfy D-07.
441	
442	**Claim inventory.** A Conclusion-section claim is a bold lead-in whose colon closes the bold span, or a numbered or bulleted list item, and the four lead-ins this template prescribes — `**Recommended approach:**`, `**Key insight:**`, `**Trade-offs acknowledged:**` and `**Confidence:**` — are always claims and each must cite a chain; the `**Confidence:**` line discharges that obligation through the chains D-07 already requires it to name, and a HIGH line whose justification prose names no chain is the one position where this rule and the extractor can disagree, so name the chain there too; nothing inside a fenced block is ever a claim whatever its shape, a near-paraphrase restatement or direct entailment of an already-cited claim earlier in the same section is not a second claim, and prose carrying neither a bold colon lead-in nor a list marker is not a claim at all. Three bounds are measured, not assumed: a bold lead-in whose colon-terminated span is the entire physical line and carries no citation of its own is a section-intro label, and the citation obligation then falls to the list items beneath it; a bold span whose closing `**` is not immediately preceded by the colon is not matched at all — write `**Label:** text` to match, not `**Label: text**`; and a list item counts only when it closes its own sentence or runs past forty characters. Enumerate by this rule, not by recollection — the rule is the contract and the extractor is a partial instrument for it.
443	
444	**Citation form.** Every Conclusion-section claim either names the chain that established it inline — `(chain C1)` — or is discharged by a §6→§4 closure ledger row that quotes the claim and names its chain. A claim doing neither is cut, not softened. Ledger discharge requires the structural row form the closure-ledger example below shows — a list marker, then the quoted claim, then an arrow, then the chain id — and a prose sentence that merely quotes something and names a chain is not a ledger row. This is detected only when the row sits inside section 6: the ledger emitted as process output in the appendix after section 6 is not visible to the check, and inline citation is therefore the mechanically checkable form.
445	
446	**Conforming — inline chain citation:**
447	
448	```text
449	**Recommended approach:** Move sustained workloads to Fargate (chain C1).
450	```
451	
452	**Conforming — closure-ledger row:**
453	
454	```text
455	- "Move sustained workloads to Fargate" → chain C1 ✓
456	```
457	
458	**Non-conforming — a claim naming no chain and quoted by no ledger row:**
459	
460	```text
461	**Recommended approach:** Move sustained workloads to Fargate.
462	```
463	
464	Both forms are accepted because both discharge the same obligation: the ledger is process output emitted in the appendix after section 6 (see the agent body — `SKILL.md` on the skill surface, `agents/first-principles.md` on the agent surface — "Before presenting conclusions"), not a seventh output section, and the chain IDs cited are the `C1`/`C2` IDs assigned by §4's chain-numbering convention.
465	
466	**Caveats.** A caveat qualifying an existing Conclusion-section claim either names the chain it qualifies inline or carries the marker `no chain — flagged assumption only` (em dash, lower case, no trailing punctuation inside the marker), and a marked caveat still scores untraced: the marker discloses the gap, it does not discharge the claim, because it is honest labelling rather than a citation and the extractor is deliberately not taught to recognise it. A caveat doing neither is cut, not softened.
467	
468	**Not a claim — a bold lead-in alone on its line, carrying no citation:**
469	
470	```text
471	**Recommended approach — three steps, in this order:**
472	```
473	
474	This is the hinge of "detectable from the emission alone" — an author can dodge extraction by putting the lead-in on its own line, and the claim obligation then falls to the numbered items beneath it.
475	
476	**A claim — the same lead-in carrying its assertion on the same line:**
477	
478	```text
479	**Recommended approach:** Move sustained workloads to Fargate before evaluating Lambda (chain C1).
480	```
481	
482	Nothing follows the closing `**` in the block above and something does here, which is the whole difference.
483	
484	**A claim — the lead-in alone on its line, but carrying its own citation:**
485	
486	```text
487	**Recommended approach, established in chain C1:**
488	```
489	
490	The section-intro-label exclusion is conditional on carrying no citation; naming the chain inside the label keeps it a claim.
491	
492	**Not matched at all — a bold span whose colon sits inside it:**
493	
494	```text
495	**Overall confidence: HIGH.**
496	```
497	
498	The extractor requires the colon to close the bold span, so this line is not a claim and not a non-claim — it is never looked at.
499	
500	**A claim — the same statement with the colon closing the bold span:**
501	
502	```text
503	**Overall confidence:** HIGH — seven of eight chains rest on figures read at source (chain C1).
504	```
505	
506	One character moved, and the statement enters the inventory.
507	
508	**Not a claim — a short list item with no sentence-ending punctuation:**
509	
510	```text
511	- Measure duty cycle first
512	```
513	
514	Twenty-four characters and no terminal punctuation, so it falls under the assertiveness floor.
515	
516	**A claim — a short list item closing its own sentence:**
517	
518	```text
519	- Size the Savings Plan after cleanup.
520	```
521	
522	Also under forty characters, so the terminal punctuation is the only thing carrying it over the floor. The two items above are worded differently only so each block is uniquely locatable by the fixture-extraction guard — a true one-character minimal pair would make one block's text a literal prefix of the other's, which no substring needle can discriminate (the `R-HEAD-PERIOD-*` lesson) — and a later control proves the axis is punctuation by re-scoring each block with its punctuation toggled.
523	
524	**Conformant but still untraced — a caveat carrying the flagged-assumption marker:**
525	
526	```text
527	**Trade-offs acknowledged:** the ~73% figure is a ceiling requiring an all-upfront commitment; the realized figure on a no-upfront plan is materially lower — no chain — flagged assumption only.
528	```
529	
530	The marker satisfies the Caveats rule above and the claim still scores untraced; that is honesty-not-score, not a defect, and it is why the extractor is not taught to recognise the marker.
531	
532	**Conformant and traced — the same caveat citing the chain it qualifies:**
533	
534	```text
535	**Trade-offs acknowledged:** the ~73% figure is a ceiling requiring an all-upfront commitment; the realized figure on a no-upfront plan is materially lower (chain C5).
536	```
537	
538	Naming C5 discharges the claim; the marker discloses it. The two rewrites land on different Criterion 6 bands, and that band is assigned by a model — no gate in this tree checks it.

3	# Self-Audit Gate
4	
5	> **Scope:** This is the Layer-3 scoring instrument read on demand by the validator-fix-repeat loop
6	> already resident in `SKILL.md`. It scores a completed first-principles analysis against the
7	> six-section output format defined in `references/output-template.md`. The loop instruction
8	> itself — when to apply, what to fix, when to stop — lives in `SKILL.md` under
9	> "Before presenting conclusions" and is **not** repeated here. Come here only to score
10	> an analysis in progress; use `SKILL.md` for the loop procedure and `output-template.md`
11	> for authoring guidance.
12	>
13	> **What this instrument scores:** the structure of *this analysis*. It is not a rubric for the
14	> subject matter. When a request asks for a rubric, scorecard, or grading scheme applied to the
15	> thing being analyzed — an article's argument, a proposal, a design — that is a **separate
16	> deliverable** that belongs in the analysis body. Producing it does not satisfy this gate, and
17	> this gate does not substitute for it. Both must appear. (Historically named the "Validation
18	> Rubric"; renamed because that name collided with subject-matter rubrics and the collision was
19	> observed to cause this gate to be skipped.)
20	
21	## How to Apply This Gate
22	
23	Score the completed analysis against all 6 criteria below. For each criterion, produce exactly
24	one verdict block in the format prescribed in the Verdict Block Format section. An analysis
25	clears this gate only when it satisfies **both** of the following conditions — clearing
26	one condition alone does not constitute a pass:
27	
28	1. **Gate cleared** — no criterion scores Absent.
29	2. **Hand-wavy cap cleared** — at most one criterion scores Hand-wavy.
30	
31	If either condition is not met, revise the analysis and re-score — bounded to **at most one re-perception pass** per analysis, per the rule stated in full under `SKILL.md`'s Turn discipline section. After that single pass, any criterion still failing — or newly failing as a result of the revision — is presented as an unresolved gap with a stated confidence caveat instead of being re-scored again.
32	
33	**Assumption Audit (verify before scoring)**
34	
35	The scan itself is not performed here — the agent already performed it at the end of Phase 4
36	(`SKILL.md`, "End-of-phase Assumption Audit") before this gate is ever applied. This
37	gate's job is narrower: verify the audit ran and its table is exhaustive, not repeat the
38	scan.
39	
40	Before scoring any criterion, confirm the audit table below is present in the analysis and
41	covers every named derivation chain step from section 4 — one row per chain per step, in
42	order, with no step skipped. Do not proceed to verdict blocks until this is confirmed. `Form conforming?` reads `unreached` where a rule binds at a position the mechanical check cannot reach — a disclosed gap in the check, never a softer `no`, and never to be scored as a conforming block. A row whose `Rule applied` cell explains that the check could not reach a position, while `Form conforming?` still reads `yes`, is scoring the block conforming on a rule it never checked; the verdict belongs in `Form conforming?`. `Band` is copied from the chain's own section-4 confidence label, so a disagreement between scan and chain is visible rather than reconciled silently. `Act attempted?` records whether the run tried to open a cited source for that chain's head inputs, and `Edges fired` which bounded re-entry edges fired for it. A load-bearing chain whose inputs are all `?`-marked and whose `Act attempted?` reads `no` is the shape this criterion most needs surfaced: a conclusion reached without once trying to check it.
43	
44	| Chain | Step | Step Text (brief) | Assumption surfaced? | Added to Table? |
45	|-------|------|-------------------|----------------------|-----------------|
46	| [chain producing conclusion X] | 1 | [step text] | [assumption or "none"] | [yes / n/a] |
47	| [chain producing conclusion X] | 2 | [step text] | [assumption or "none"] | [yes / n/a] |
48	| [chain producing conclusion Y] | 1 | [step text] | [assumption or "none"] | [yes / n/a] |
49

120	## Scoring Model
121	
122	Score each of the 6 criteria using this shared 4-level scale, applied uniformly across all criteria
123	(highest to lowest):
124	
125	- **Rigorous** — the criterion's named artifact is present, structurally complete, and every
126	  entry meets the observable descriptor for this level: all required fields are populated with
127	  non-generic content, all required relationships are explicit,
128	  and every observable structural test in this criterion's Rigorous descriptor returns pass.
129	
130	- **Sound** — the criterion's named artifact is present and mostly meets the Rigorous descriptor,
131	  but one or more entries fall short in a specific, identifiable way: a field is generic or vague
132	  rather than empty, a relationship is implicit rather than absent, or one entry departs from the
133	  prescribed form without invalidating the rest.
134	
135	- **Hand-wavy** — the criterion's named artifact is present but fails the Rigorous descriptor in
136	  a pattern rather than an isolated entry: multiple fields are generic or empty, the artifact's
137	  prescribed structure is not followed, or the section uses the honest-depth escape valve with a
138	  reason that could be copy-pasted to any analysis without modification.
139	
140	- **Absent** — the criterion's named artifact is missing entirely, or the section exists but
141	  contains no content that could be scored against the artifact's descriptor (the section heading
142	  appears with nothing substantive below it).
143	
144	**Rank order (explicit):** Rigorous > Sound > Hand-wavy > Absent.
145	
146	**Gate:** Any criterion scored **Absent** fails the entire analysis — it must be revised and
147	re-scored, bounded to at most one re-perception pass per analysis, per "How to Apply This
148	Gate" above. If the criterion still scores Absent after that single pass, it is presented as
149	an unresolved gap with a stated confidence caveat instead of being withheld, regardless of how
150	all other criteria score.
151	
152	**Hand-wavy cap:** Two or more criteria scored **Hand-wavy** also fails the entire analysis —
153	the same bound applies: revise and re-score once, per "How to Apply This Gate" above. One
154	criterion at Hand-wavy is tolerated (one isolated weaker section does not indicate a systemic
155	quality problem); two or more at Hand-wavy indicates a pattern of shallow reasoning that the
156	gate alone cannot catch, because no single criterion has reached the gate-fail level. If two or
157	more criteria still score Hand-wavy after that single pass, the cap breach is presented as an
158	unresolved gap with a stated confidence caveat instead of being withheld.
159	
160	**Pass:** No criterion scores Absent, and at most one criterion scores Hand-wavy.
161	(Equivalently: every criterion is Sound or above, except at most one may be Hand-wavy.)
162	
163	**Escape-valve scoring (global rule, applies to every criterion):** Any section that
164	legitimately uses the honest-depth escape valve (`Nothing material here — [reason]`) is
165	scored **Rigorous** if the stated reason is specific to this analysis — it names a property
166	of this problem that makes the section's content unnecessary — and **Hand-wavy** if the
167	reason is generic or copy-pasteable to any analysis. A properly-used escape valve is
168	**never** scored Absent solely for using the escape valve: the per-criterion Absent
169	descriptors below apply to a section that is missing, empty, or filled with non-scoreable
170	content, not to a section that is honestly and specifically marked as having no material
171	content.
172	
173	**Load-bearing chain (definition):** A derivation chain is *load-bearing* if a claim in
174	the Conclusion section (output section 6) depends on it — i.e., the chain produces, or is
175	cited as support for, a conclusion the analysis actually presents. A chain that reaches
176	only an intermediate result no conclusion rests on is not load-bearing. (This is the
177	narrower scoring sense of the phrase `SKILL.md` uses informally as "load-bearing for a
178	high-stakes conclusion.")

## 3. Ground Truths

- **GT-1** NYC Local Law 144 (effective July 5, 2023) requires a covered employer/employment agency using an automated employment decision tool (AEDT) to obtain an independent bias audit within the year prior to use and to publicly "post a summary of the results of the bias audit," plus give candidates advance notice — it does not require publication of the underlying training data or a list of training-data sources. — source: NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, AEDT page (nyc.gov/site/dca/about/automated-employment-decision-tools.page); read-at-source: page text quoting the posting duty as "Post a summary of the results of the bias audit."

- **GT-3** Among the bias-audit reports that were publicly posted under GT-1's regime, roughly 96% reported impact ratios at or above the EEOC's four-fifths (0.8) threshold — i.e., showed no statistical adverse impact — a pattern the researchers attribute to selective, litigation-avoidant disclosure rather than to AEDTs being uniformly unbiased. — source: same arxiv paper as GT-2; read-at-source: "96% of published audit reports showed impact ratios above the 0.8 threshold."
- **GT-4?** Under Title VII, algorithmic hiring tools are treated as "selection procedures"; disparate/adverse impact is assessed by comparing selection rates across protected groups, using the "four-fifths rule" (a group's selection rate below 80% of the highest group's rate) as a rule-of-thumb screening threshold under the 1979 Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures — i.e., the operative legal test is a comparison of outcome statistics, not an inquiry into which organizations supplied the training data. — cited to: EEOC technical guidance ("Select Issues: Assessing Adverse Impact...") and 29 CFR 1607; reported-by-delegate: law-firm summaries (Mayer Brown, Ogletree) returned by WebSearch — cited sources not opened successfully by this analysis (see Phase 3 failure records below).

127	## 6. Conclusion
128	
129	**Recommended approach:** Read the proposed rule as it is most likely to be implemented — a bare "publish training data sources" duty without a mandated statistical/outcome schema, independent verification, or enforcement funding (A6, A7, A9) — and expect three things to actually follow: categorical, low-specificity vendor disclosures rather than itemized data-source accounting (chain C1); a source-of-training-data disclosure that, however complete, cannot by itself reveal discriminatory bias, because bias is a property of outcome/feature statistics that source-naming does not convey (chain C2); and real-world compliance that is low and self-selected toward favorable results, mirroring the closest existing analogue (chain C3). Taken together, the rule as commonly proposed would generate compliance activity and modest secondary transparency value but would not, on the evidence assembled here, achieve the anti-discrimination/accountability aim usually invoked to justify it (chains C1, C2, C3).
130	
131	**Key insight:** The rule's likely failure mode is not weak enforcement alone — it is a structural tension between two goals commonly bundled together under "AI hiring transparency." The specificity that would make a data-source disclosure diagnostic of bias (chain C2) is largely the same specificity that collides with data-protection law's purpose-limitation and minimization principles for the real people whose records are in that data (chain C4) — so the version of the disclosure that would be most useful for the stated aim is also the version regulators and firms have the strongest independent reasons not to require or publish.
132	
133	**Trade-offs acknowledged:** A source-publication duty is not worthless: it can create secondary value for copyright/privacy enforcement and for researchers cross-referencing named datasets against independently documented bias properties in the narrow cases where those exist (chain C2), and its likely low real-world compliance mirrors a documented pattern in the closest existing analogue rather than a flaw unique to this proposal (chain C3). Adopting this design over a more direct instrument also risks crowding out political appetite for outcome-based bias audits with independent verification and enforcement funding — the instrument the evidence here suggests is the closer fit to the stated aim — no chain — flagged assumption only.
